\chapter{The Regular Preterite}
\label{ch:spanish-preterito-regular}
\hlchaptermodality{45}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I did with a regular -er or -ir verb, and place the written accent correctly.}

-er and -ir agree again, and the accent marks the stressed final vowel.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[comí]{comí — one regular -er singular past}

\label{lesson:ES-C15-comer-preterite}



\begin{quote}
You know present \textbf{como, comes, come} and the singular \textbf{-ar} past. To make a completed past from \textbf{comer}, keep \textbf{com-} and learn three forms: \textbf{comí, comiste, comió}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: present beside completed past}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present} & \textbf{completed past} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{como} & \textbf{comí} \\
tú & \textbf{comes} & \textbf{comiste} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{come} & \textbf{comió} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{comí · comiste · comió}. Keep the limit visible: these are the same three familiar singular persons. Plural forms wait.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: final stress in two forms}]
\textbf{Comí} and \textbf{comió} carry written accents because their stress falls on the final vowel. \textbf{Comiste} follows ordinary next-to-last stress, so it needs no mark. The three forms by themselves make complete utterances:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Comí.} — “I ate.”
  \item \textbf{¿Comiste?} — “Did you eat?”
  \item \textbf{Comió.} — “He, she, or you-formal ate.”
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Spanish \textbf{comer} continues Latin \textbf{comedere}. Its regular past endings also continue Latin perfect material, including forms with \textbf{-ī, -istī, -it}. Sound change and analogy reshaped that material across Romance into Spanish \textbf{-í, -iste, -ió}. The resemblance is real, but it is not one tidy chain in which every modern ending merely drops a letter.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “comí, comiste, comió”
  \item “Como. Comí.”
  \item “comí and comió carry final-stress accents”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three learned \textbf{comer} forms. (\emph{Comí, comiste, comió.}) Which carry written accents? (\emph{Comí} and \emph{comió}.) What shaped the modern endings? (Latin perfect material, sound change, and analogy.) Next: reuse the same endings with a known \textbf{-ir} verb.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[viví]{viví — reuse one past pattern with an -ir verb}

\label{lesson:ES-C15-comer-vivir-preterite}



\begin{quote}
You know present \textbf{vivo, vives, vive}, and you just learned past \textbf{comí, comiste, comió}. Keep \textbf{viv-} and reuse those three past endings: \textbf{viví, viviste, vivió}.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one -ir singular past}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present} & \textbf{completed past} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{vivo} & \textbf{viví} \\
tú & \textbf{vives} & \textbf{viviste} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{vive} & \textbf{vivió} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{viví · viviste · vivió}. Reuse known \textbf{en} for a small contrast:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Vivo en Madrid.} — “I live in Madrid.”
  \item \textbf{Viví en Madrid.} — “I lived in Madrid.”
  \item \textbf{¿Viviste en Madrid?} — “Did you live in Madrid?”
  \item \textbf{Vivió en Madrid.} — “He, she, or you-formal lived in Madrid.”
\end{itemize}

The written accents in \textbf{viví} and \textbf{vivió} show final stress. \textbf{Viviste} already has ordinary next-to-last stress and needs no mark.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: -er and -ir meet in this past}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{\textbf{comer}} & \textbf{\textbf{vivir}} \\
\midrule
yo & com\textbf{í} & viv\textbf{í} \\
tú & com\textbf{iste} & viv\textbf{iste} \\
él / ella / usted & com\textbf{ió} & viv\textbf{ió} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The shared endings are \textbf{-í} in the first row, \textbf{-iste} in the second, and \textbf{-ió} in the third. The presents differ, but these two singular past rows converge on one ending set. That is a fact about the forms you have learned, not permission to guess plural forms; those wait.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Spanish \textbf{vivir} continues Latin \textbf{vīvere}. Its modern past endings belong to the same Romance history as the \textbf{comer} endings: Latin perfect material was reshaped by sound change and analogy. The shared \textbf{-iste} is a useful family resemblance, not proof of one simple letter-by-letter erosion.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “viví, viviste, vivió”
  \item “Vivo en Madrid. Viví en Madrid.”
  \item “comí and viví share -í; comió and vivió share -ió”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the three learned \textbf{vivir} forms. (\emph{Viví, viviste, vivió.}) Which past endings do \textbf{comer} and \textbf{vivir} share? (\emph{-í, -iste, -ió.}) Which two carry written accents? (\emph{Viví} and \emph{vivió}.) Next, keep the singular limit but let the stem change.
\end{tcolorbox}
